newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Krupp-Thyssen wins Bonn support, insider probe.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Krupp-Thyssen wins Bonn support, insider probe.

text.p: A possible steel tie-up between German industrial groups Thyssen and Krupp won support from Bonn on Friday, but also drew calls from a regional state for a probe into possible insider trading.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said that merging the steel operations of Thyssen AG and Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp was inevitable and would be good for the industry.

"The goal of all efforts must be to strengthen the competitiveness of the German steel industry and to secure jobs," he told a conference in the industrial city of Gelsenkirchen. "Germany must keep its steel base."
Talks opened this week on a mutually acceptable deal after Krupp suspended its hostile takeover bid for Thyssen.
But speculation surfaced on Friday that Krupp might not have given up yet on the bid. Banking sources said institutional investors might have secured a large packet of Thyssen shares for Krupp.
Krupp chairman Gerhard Cromme and Thyssen chief Dieter Vogel were expected to continue meeting over the weekend.
Sources at Krupp said its supervisory board would meet on Saturday but the company would not officially comment.
The state government of North Rhine-Westphalia, where most of Gremany's steel industry is based, has criticised the role of banks in supporting Krupp's bid.
On Friday it called for a probe into possible insider trading violations. "The responsible parties have to exercise due diligence," said state finance minister Heinz Scheusser.
Some of Krupp's advising banks also sit on Thyssen's supervisory board. Thyssen denied any board members had done anything wrong.
Scheusser's announcement came after newspapers reported that Krupp had gained control of 30 percent of Thyssen through institutional investors. Krupp denied this.

Germany's BAWe securities watchdog said it had not been notified of any accumulation of Thyssen stock exceeding five percent, the legal threshold for disclosure, and had no indications of any related insider trading offences.

Krupp's bid for Thyssen is backed by Germany's two largest banks, Deutsche and Dresdner Bank, and U.S. investment house Goldman Sachs. It suspended the offer after Thyssen agreed to talks about forming a joint steel company.
Rexrodt, a member of the Free Democrat (FDP) junior coalition partner, said the talks were going well.
Others close to the deal said Krupp, even without a base of Thyssen shares in hand, was determined to use a fusion with Thyssen to produce a reinvigorated German steel giant.
"The company is determined to bring about something new in Germany," said one source close to the deal.
A Dresdner Bank spokesman said: "We welcome Krupp's initiative to secure a merger. We think it is a positive move."

Thyssen has few large blocks of stock owned by shareholders that it could count on to help ward off a takeover. Insurer Allianz AG, which owns eight percent of Thyssen's stock, has said it is considering the Krupp bid.
Krupp offered Thyssen shareholders 435 marks per share, 25 percent more than the stock price at the time and 60 percent over the price of the shares at the end of 1996.
Thyssen shares ended floor trading on Friday at 391 marks, up 15.20. Krupp shares closed up four at 317 marks.

With 9.5 billion marks in steel sales, Thyssen is the top German steel maker, but only number five in Europe. Krupp has 5.2 billion marks in steel revenue. Together the companies would rival Europe's two largest steel makers, France's Unisor Sacilor and British Steel Plc.

North Rhine-Westphalia, home of both Krupp and Thyssen, hoped a deal creating a world-class steel maker would revitalise its depressed coal and steel industries and result in fewer job losses than a hostile takeover.

"In a merger you wouldn't have thousands of workers put on the street at the same time. The necessary job cuts would take place as socially as possible," said state economics minister Wolfgang Clement.
